clinical_guidelines.title: Preoperative and Perioperative Considerations for EC and APC
clinical_guidelines.condition: Central airway disease/endoluminal obstruction requiring electrocautery (EC) or argon plasma coagulation (APC)
specific_recommendations: Place a grounding pad on the patient; remove jewelry and metallic objects.
Patients with implantable electronic cardiac devices should undergo preoperative evaluation by anesthesia when feasible.
For pacemaker-dependent patients, place a magnet for a fixed cardiac pace; deprogram and reprogram defibrillators for the procedure.
Avoid EC and APC if a patient cannot tolerate asynchronous mode.
Ensure FiO2 <40% (or 3 LPM or lower for conscious sedation) before firing to reduce airway fire risk.
If FiO2 cannot be reduced to <40% (or 3 LPM), pursue alternative nonthermal options.
Alternate cutting (yellow) and coagulation (blue) foot pedals as needed.
Apply suction during activation to remove smoke.
Monitor vital signs closely; pause EC/APC for transient oxygen desaturations to allow brief FiO2 increase and recovery.
Mechanically debulk/remove thermally destroyed tissue (e.g., forceps or cryoprobe) via rigid or flexible bronchoscope.
decision_points_and_pathways: If pacemaker-dependent → place magnet for fixed pacing; if defibrillator present → deprogram for procedure then reprogram post-procedure.
If patient cannot tolerate asynchronous mode → avoid EC/APC.
Before firing: if ventilated FiO2 cannot be reduced <40% (or 3 LPM for conscious sedation) → use nonthermal alternatives.
During desaturation → pause EC/APC, briefly increase FiO2, resume after recovery.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients undergoing EC or APC for endoluminal central airway disease, including those with implantable cardiac devices.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Avoid EC/APC if a patient cannot tolerate asynchronous mode or if FiO2 cannot be safely reduced to <40% (or 3 LPM for conscious sedation).
clinical_guidelines.monitoring_requirements: Monitor vital signs closely; manage transient oxygen desaturations with procedural breaks and temporary FiO2 increases.
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: Use nonthermal options if FiO2 cannot be reduced below thresholds.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: It is essential that the FiO2 for ventilated patients is less than 40% (or 3 LPM or lower for conscious sedation patients) to reduce the risk of iatrogenic airway fire.

clinical_guidelines.title: Indications and Contraindications for EC and APC
clinical_guidelines.condition: Central airway disease (benign or malignant) with endoluminal obstruction
specific_recommendations: Use EC and APC for endoluminal management of central airway disease of benign and malignant etiologies.
Do not use EC/APC for obstruction or narrowing caused by extrinsic compression alone.
For mixed endoluminal and extrinsic lesions, consider a multimodal approach combining ablative therapies with airway stenting or dilation.
decision_points_and_pathways: Extrinsic compression alone → EC/APC not indicated.
Mixed endoluminal + extrinsic → consider combining ablation with stenting or dilation.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Obstructive disease of benign and malignant etiologies provided the obstruction is endoluminal in nature.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Not indicated for obstruction or narrowing caused by extrinsic compression alone.
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: Airway stenting or dilation in combination for complex mixed lesions.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: EC and APC are not indicated for obstruction or narrowing of the airways caused by extrinsic compression alone.

clinical_guidelines.title: Electrocautery (EC) Treatment Strategy and Initial Settings
clinical_guidelines.condition: Endobronchial lesions/central airway obstruction treated with EC
specific_recommendations: Use direct contact to cut or coagulate; apply suction during activation to remove smoke.
Typical initial settings: power 20–60 W with long duration (high cutting) and low effect (low coagulation).
Both resection and coagulation can be achieved simultaneously by EC.
decision_points_and_pathways: Adjust power, duration, interval, and effect to control tissue impact.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Typical initial settings include a power of 20–60 W with a long duration (high cutting) and low effect (low coagulation).

clinical_guidelines.title: Needle Knife Technique for Webs/Stenosis
clinical_guidelines.condition: Circumferential airway disease or short-segment webs/stenosis
specific_recommendations: Make several short interval cuts rather than one prolonged cut to avoid airway perforation.
Target multiple radial locations (e.g., 12, 3, and 9 o’clock) for circumferential release of webs or stenosis.
Avoid targeting the posterior airway wall to prevent esophageal perforation.
decision_points_and_pathways: Circumferential disease present → perform radial cuts at multiple positions; avoid posterior wall.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with circumferential airway disease or short-segment webs/stenosis.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Do not cut the posterior wall to avoid esophageal perforation.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The posterior wall of the airway is not targeted to avoid esophageal perforation.

clinical_guidelines.title: Snare Use for Pedunculated Tumors
clinical_guidelines.condition: Pedunculated endobronchial tumors with a visible stalk
specific_recommendations: Wrap the snare around the base of the stalk, tighten, then activate electrocautery.
Repeat sequential bursts to excise and coagulate until the tumor is released and mechanically removed.
decision_points_and_pathways: Pedunculated tumor with visible stalk → snare tightening and EC activation in bursts → remove released tumor.
clinical_guidelines.patient_population_criteria: Patients with pedunculated tumors with a visible stalk.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The snare is typically used for pedunculated tumors with a visible stalk and is wrapped around the base of the stalk of the tumor like a lasso.

clinical_guidelines.title: Hot Forceps Use and Limitations
clinical_guidelines.condition: Endobronchial or transbronchial biopsy with coagulation
specific_recommendations: Hot forceps deliver coagulative heat during biopsy to decrease bleeding risk conceptually.
Studies have not shown significant bleeding reduction versus traditional forceps; rarely employed in modern practice.
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: Traditional forceps for biopsy when bleeding reduction is not demonstrated.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: studies have not demonstrated a significant reduction compared to traditional forceps. As a result, the hot forceps is rarely employed in modern interventional pulmonology practice.

clinical_guidelines.title: Blunt Probe Application and Safety
clinical_guidelines.condition: Airway lesions requiring direct-contact cauterization/ablation or bleeding control
specific_recommendations: Apply blunt probe for destruction/cauterization by direct contact; can control bleeding or ablate tumor.
Avoid long activations to prevent perforation or airway injury.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Avoid prolonged energy activation to prevent perforation or injury.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: Care must be taken to avoid long activations of energy as this can result in perforation or injury of the airway.

clinical_guidelines.title: APC Treatment Strategy – Initial Power and Gas Flow Settings
clinical_guidelines.condition: Superficial mucosal lesions and malignant/benign endobronchial disease treated with APC
specific_recommendations: Typical initial APC settings: power 20–40 Watts and argon gas flow 0.3–1.8 L/min.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The typical initial settings for APC include a power of 20–40 Watts and argon gas flow between 0.3 and 1.8 L/min.

clinical_guidelines.title: APC Gas Flow Limit to Reduce Air Embolism Risk
clinical_guidelines.condition: APC use where gas flow is adjustable
specific_recommendations: Gas flow >1 L/min linked to increased air embolism risk; keep APC gas flow less than 1 L/min.
decision_points_and_pathways: If considering higher gas flow → maintain <1 L/min to reduce embolism risk.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Avoid APC gas flow >1 L/min due to increased air embolism risk.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: A gas flow >1 L/min has been linked to an increased risk of air embolism; therefore, it is recommended to keep the gas flow less than 1 L/min.

clinical_guidelines.title: APC Probe Positioning to Prevent Scope Damage
clinical_guidelines.condition: APC delivered via flexible or rigid bronchoscopy
specific_recommendations: Keep APC probe tip both distal and visible to the bronchoscope tip by approximately 2 cm to prevent scope damage.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The probe tip must remain both distal and visible to the tip of the bronchoscope by approximately 2 cm to prevent damage and burning of the bronchoscope.

clinical_guidelines.title: APC Targeting Distance and Activation Technique
specific_recommendations: Aim APC within 1–3 mm of the target lesion.
Activate in short bursts with a painting motion until a devitalized, necrotic eschar is produced.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: The APC is then aimed within 1–3 mm of the target lesion and activated with a foot petal in short bursts with a painting motion across the lesion

clinical_guidelines.title: APC Noncontact Technique to Reduce Air Embolism
clinical_guidelines.condition: APC usage where air embolism risk is a concern
specific_recommendations: Use APC in a noncontact method: target tissue closest to the probe but not in actual contact.
Noncontact use decreases the risk of air embolism from argon gas.
decision_points_and_pathways: When firing APC → ensure noncontact to minimize embolism risk.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: the APC probe be used in a noncontact method when fired such that the target tissue is closest to the probe but not in actual contact with it.

clinical_guidelines.title: FiO2 Requirement for Thermal Modalities
clinical_guidelines.condition: Use of EC, APC, or laser for airway disease
specific_recommendations: All three modalities require FiO2 less than 40% to decrease the risk of airway fire.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Do not proceed if FiO2 cannot be reduced below 40% (thermal fire risk).
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: Consider nonthermal modalities when FiO2 cannot be lowered.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: All three modalities require an FiO2 of less than 40% to decrease the risk of airway fire

clinical_guidelines.title: Alternative Therapies – Cryotherapy Selection Considerations
clinical_guidelines.condition: Airway tumors where delayed ablation and high FiO2 may be considerations
specific_recommendations: Cryotherapy preserves bronchial cartilage with less scar tissue formation.
Cryotherapy does not have the risk of ignition and can be used in high FiO2 environments.
Tissue ablation is delayed by days or weeks; inappropriate when immediate recanalization is required.
decision_points_and_pathways: If high FiO2 required or desire to preserve cartilage → consider cryotherapy.
If immediate recanalization needed → do not use cryotherapy alone.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Cryotherapy alone inappropriate when immediate airway recanalization is required.
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: Rapid ablative techniques (APC, EC, laser) for immediate recanalization.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: cryotherapy does not have the risk of ignition and can be used in high FiO2 environments. However, tissue ablation is delayed by days or weeks

clinical_guidelines.title: Alternative Therapies – Brachytherapy and Photodynamic Therapy (PDT)
clinical_guidelines.condition: Palliative management or carcinoma in situ where delayed modalities considered
specific_recommendations: Brachytherapy is complex and expensive; cannot provide immediate improvement in airway emergencies.
In modern practice, brachytherapy has seen a significant decline in use and has almost no application.
PDT can be used for curative intent for carcinoma in situ or palliative management of malignant central airway disease.
PDT therapeutic effects are typically delayed by 48 hours.
decision_points_and_pathways: Airway emergency needing immediate improvement → do not use brachytherapy.
Carcinoma in situ or palliative malignant CAO → consider PDT with awareness of 48-hour delay.
clinical_guidelines.contraindications_and_exceptions: Brachytherapy not suitable for airway emergencies due to need for several treatment fractions.
clinical_guidelines.alternative_approaches: Rapid ablative techniques (APC, EC, laser) for immediate relief.
clinical_guidelines.source_excerpt: PDT does not provide immediate relief of airway obstruction, and the therapeutic effects are typically delayed by 48 hours.

figures.caption: Fig. 1 A patient with a history of prolonged intubation and tracheostomy presented 1 year after tracheostomy decannulation due to progressive shortness of breath. (a) Airway exam demonstrated >50% subglottic stenosis. (b and c) Several precise radial cuts of the short segment web were achieved with electrocautery via a needle knife, with particular care to avoid deep cuts in the posterior membrane to avoid esophageal perforation. (d) The airway was dilated with a continuous radial expansion (CRE) balloon with improved luminal airway diameter and symptom burden
key_findings: Several precise radial cuts of the short segment web were achieved with electrocautery via a needle knife.
Care was taken to avoid deep cuts in the posterior membrane to avoid esophageal perforation.
The airway was dilated with a continuous radial expansion (CRE) balloon.
Improved luminal airway diameter and symptom burden.
figures.clinical_significance: Improved luminal airway diameter and symptom burden.

definitions.content: is the use of an electrical current to heat the target tissue with direct contact of an electrical instrument, allowing immediate destruction of endobronchial disease.

clinical_pearls.content: Because the argon plasma stream conducts electrons toward the closest tissue surface, APC can be directed around corners to follow the angulations of segmental bronchial tree branches.
clinical_pearls.source_excerpt: APC can be directed around corners to follow the angulations of segmental bronchial tree branches.
